citation.title: Exchanging access goods for access: A comparative study of business lobbying in the European Union institutions
citation.venue_or_publisher: European Journal of Political Research, Volume 43, Issue 3, pp. 337-369 (Cambridge Core page)
citation.type: journal article; only the Cambridge Core landing page with abstract and reference links is in the file

question: Tests empirically a theory of access: why business interests (companies, associations, consultants) get access to the European Commission, European Parliament and Council of Ministers, explained as supply and demand of access goods.
data: Per the abstract: 126 exploratory and semi-structured interviews in the EU financial services sector. Nothing further on period or sampling is in the file.
method: Per the abstract: specific hypotheses about access are checked across the three EU institutions against interview data. No further method detail is in the file.

definitions.definition: Information that is crucial in the EU policy-making process, which business interests must supply in return for access to an EU institution.
definitions.quote: Access goods concern information that is crucial in the EU policy‐making process.

definitions.term: Organizational forms of business interest representation
definitions.definition: Three forms named in the abstract: companies, associations and consultants. No criteria for deciding what counts as business are in the file.
definitions.quote: the access of different organizational forms of business interest representation – companies, associations and consultants – to the European Commission

limitations.point: The file holds only the abstract and a reference list (links); the full text is not present, and the reference list shows as loading. Nothing beyond the abstract is recorded. The access page shows article purchase as temporarily unavailable.
The extracted text has no author field; the author name is taken from a link anchor and the copyright link on the page.
